newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Country Road won't call 96/7 profit.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Country Road won't call 96/7 profit.

text.p: Clothing and homewares retailer Country Road Ltd said on Thursday that its first half performance was disappointing as expected and while it hoped for a second half improvement, would not predict full year earnings.

"I think it would be totally improper for me to speculate on that at the moment," chief executive Mike Howell said when asked to forecast the 1996/97 profit. "All I can say is that we had a disappointing first half, the second half is patchy," he said.
The company said earlier that first half net profit before abnormals was 45 percent lower at A$3.04 million, a touch better than the January forecast that profit could be 50 percent lower.
Sales in the six months to February 2 fell 6.4 percent to A$136.96 million. The company told shareholders two months ago that the key Christmas period had been the worst on record.
Howell said he was hopeful that the sales fall could be reversed, noting an improvement in the U.S. operations where Itochu Corp last month took a 25 percent stake for an outlay of US$4 million.
Losses from the U.S. operations eased to A$300,000 from A$1.6 million a year ago on a sales rise of 12.5 percent.
In contrast, sales from the much larger Australia and New Zealand units fell by a total of 8.2 percent.
He said the company partly misread the apparel market during the first six months of 1996/97.
"There has been a well document change in consumer spending patterns and we think that in the long haul that our product is quite well suited to that because it is of a less formal nature.

"Obviously we are conscious of the fact that our merchandise wasn't spot-on during the summer season and where it is appropriate we have tried to make modifications to our styling," said Howell, who spoke to Reuters after an analysts briefing.

Howell said he kept in regular contact with major shareholders, including Peter Lew who last month revealed he had a 9.23 percent stake and who is not regarded as a passive investor by analysts or traders.
Lew is the son of Solomon Lew, the major shareholder in leading retailer Coles Myer Ltd.
Peter Lew said last month that a takeover of Country Road was not imminent but added that he would take a keen interest in the first half profit result.
In response to the Lew shareholding, Country Road chairman Bill Loewenthal said in a statement accompanying the profit result that the company did not plan a share placement.
Howell said he certainly hoped Lew was not a predator.

"There has obviously been a lot of speculation about it. And as has been documented they asked us to have a look at the Witchery business but frankly we don't believe that the two are compatible and that is a different issue altogether."
Recent media reports said the privately-held Voyager group of Solomon Lew had asked Country Road to consider buying the 70 Witchery stores which are aimed a a more downmarket client base.
The Australian Financial Review said earlier this month that the sale price was about A$35 million.
Country Road shares were untraded on Thursday, and ended two cents lower on Wednesday at A$1.78. With 52 million shares on issue, the company is valued at A$92.55 million.
It achieved 1995/96 net profits of A$10.17 million on sales of A$278.19 million.
-- Ian Pemberton, Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
